_note: What the player sees along each flight. Facts marked with a source come from that NASA document; the rest are general background.

mars.name: Earth
facts: The Atlas V first stage burns for about 4 minutes, then the Centaur upper stage fires twice.
The spacecraft separates less than an hour after liftoff, moving at about 11,000 m/s.

mars.name: The Moon
facts: Earth’s Moon is about 384,000 km away.
A Mars mission passes its orbit within a day or two and keeps going.

mars.name: The Sun
facts: Earth, Mars and your spacecraft all orbit the Sun.
The trip to Mars is about half an orbit around the Sun, called a transfer orbit.

mars.name: Venus
mars.role: Inside Earth’s orbit, not on this path
facts: Some missions use Venus for a gravity assist.
A direct Mars trip heads outward, away from Venus.

mars.name: Deep-space cruise
facts: Five trajectory correction manoeuvres were planned for MRO’s cruise.
Navigators track the spacecraft with the Deep Space Network’s antennas in California, Spain and Australia.

mars.name: Mars
facts: Mars averages 227.7 million km from the Sun, about 1.5 times farther than Earth.
Its gravity is 38% of Earth’s and a day lasts 24 h 39 min.

mars.name: Orbit insertion
facts: MRO fired its six main engines for about 25 minutes to slow down by about 1,000 m/s and be captured by Mars.
Afterwards it used aerobraking, dipping into the upper atmosphere for about six months, to shrink its orbit.

mars.name: Data comes home
facts: Orbiters like MRO never come back to Earth: the science returns as radio signals.
At Mars’ farthest, MRO sent about 600 kilobits per second to a 34 m antenna; signals take up to about 21 minutes.

lander.name: Earth
facts: InSight launched on an Atlas V, the first planetary launch from California’s west coast.
The whole spacecraft weighed about 694 kg at launch.

lander.name: The Moon
facts: About 384,000 km from Earth.
The lander passes its orbit and keeps going toward Mars.

lander.name: The Sun
facts: The cruise to Mars is about half an orbit around the Sun.
Sunlight at Mars is weaker, so the lander’s round arrays make 600–700 W on a clear day.

lander.name: Venus
facts: Venus orbits closer to the Sun than Earth.
Mars missions head outward, away from it.

lander.name: Mars
facts: Gravity is 38% of Earth’s, and the air is less than 1% as thick.
Thin air is why a lander needs a heat shield, a parachute and engines.

lander.name: Cruise stage separation
facts: The cruise stage is dropped. What is left, the aeroshell with the lander inside, is called the entry vehicle.
It turns to put its heat shield forward; the turn takes about 70 seconds.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Entry interface
facts: InSight hits the top of the atmosphere at about 5.5 km/s with about 608 kg of entry mass.
The target window there is only about 10 km by 24 km after a 479 million km trip.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Peak heating
facts: The outside of the heat shield reaches about 1,500 °C.
Friction removes nearly 99.5% of the vehicle’s energy of motion before the parachute opens.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Peak deceleration
facts: Up to 7.5 g: more than seven times the pull of Earth’s gravity.
Hot ionised gas around the vehicle can briefly block the radio signal.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Parachute opens
facts: The 11.8 m parachute opens at about 385 m/s.
The first jolt pulls with about 55,600 newtons.

lander.name: Heat shield off, legs out
facts: The heat shield is dropped and the three legs extend.
About a minute before landing, the radar starts measuring speed and height.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Lander separation
facts: The lander drops away from the back shell and parachute about 45 seconds before touchdown.
One second later its 12 descent engines start firing.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Constant-velocity descent
facts: The lander switches to a steady, slow descent for the last 50 metres.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Touchdown
facts: Sensors on the legs feel the ground and shut off the engines.
The whole entry, descent and landing takes about 6.5 minutes: the ‘seven minutes of terror’.
lander.source: JPL InSight landing press kit, mission overview

lander.name: Data comes home
facts: Landers stay on Mars. InSight sent its data home directly and through orbiters.
Dust on the arrays slowly cut its power: 200–300 W on dusty days.

moon.name: Earth
facts: LRO launched on an Atlas V 401 in 2009.
The Atlas V limit for LRO was 2,000 kg; LRO was designed at about 1,845 kg.
moon.source: NASA GSFC LRO mission design paper

moon.name: The Sun
facts: The Moon is about as far from the Sun as Earth, so the arrays get full sunlight.
Shadows behind the Moon are what the battery is for.

moon.name: Translunar cruise
facts: The trip to the Moon takes about five days.
Total Δv for LRO was about 1,258 m/s.

moon.name: The Moon
facts: About 384,000 km from Earth.
LRO braked by about 555 m/s to enter a 50 km polar orbit.

moon.name: Data comes home
facts: LRO stays at the Moon and sends its maps home by radio.
Its Ka-band link reached 100 megabits per second.

europa.name: Earth
facts: Europa Clipper launched on a Falcon Heavy weighing about 5,800 kg, almost half of it propellant.

europa.name: The Sun
facts: Jupiter is about five times farther from the Sun than Earth, so sunlight there is only about 4% as strong.
That is why Clipper’s arrays are so large.

europa.name: Mars flyby
facts: Clipper swings past Mars to steal a little of its orbital speed.
Gravity assists save propellant that a rocket alone could not carry.

europa.name: Earth flyby
facts: Back past Earth for one more push outward toward Jupiter.

europa.name: Asteroid belt
facts: Between Mars and Jupiter. Asteroids are so far apart that spacecraft cross the belt without dodging.

europa.name: Jupiter
facts: Jupiter’s radiation belts would destroy normal electronics.
Clipper keeps its electronics in a vault with walls up to 9.2 mm thick.

europa.name: Europa
facts: An icy moon with an ocean under its shell.
Clipper orbits Jupiter and dives past Europa again and again instead of orbiting it, to limit radiation.

europa.name: Data comes home
facts: Clipper stays at Jupiter. Each flyby’s data is stored, then sent home by radio.
